"There is something wrong with breaking the law, even when it's corrupt."

Why do you think that?

Because law is the bedrock of civilization. Without it, we'd be reduced to a combination of roving marauder tribes and sedentary settlements that would only be cohesive within themselves because the people there obey rules. Otherwise known as laws.

People think that anarchy as a state of civilization is total lawlessness, but that can't be. Human beings naturally come up with rules. Even the roving bands of marauders would have their rules. Anarchy means lower density of lands occupied by sedentary people obeying rules, and more diversity of rules between. So, if laws always exist then they will always be formulated by people and will therefore reflect values.

Corruption's primary operating principle is that it coexists with law. Without rules formed of values that in turn imply their own courtesies, the term "corruption" means nothing. There would be nothing to corrupt! So, to say that corruption invalidates law is to say that law is forever invalid.

Were that functionally true in effect then we wouldn't be having this conversation because humanity would never have progressed beyond anarchy. In fact, through divine right naming kings to form nations via a then often power hungry and amoral Catholic Church, Western Civilization was rebuilt post-Rome as much upon corruption as law.

This is not to say that corruption is a good thing. It's just the other side of the coin. The struggle is therefore determining what specifically should be deemed corruption so that it may be corrected. That's not always as simple as it may seem in concept, so the next thing is to ensure that those making that discernment reflect the values of the civilization.

Take, for example, that China has recently taken a harsh stand against marital infidelity as part of their countermeasures against corruption. In the United States, we value liberty over tradition so that would be deemed a corruption of the system here. In China, where a unified tradition is of greater cultural importance, it's exactly the opposite. Corruption, like law, only has meaning relative to a culture.

That's where our problems lie. It's not so much that the ruling factions have no values, but that as a civilization we are so diverse in people and subcultures that there are too many value systems to represent well. As a result, there will always be subcultures who feel that corruption is going unchecked, and there will always be some measure of friction there.

The most realistic goal is to achieve a state where the worst complaints do not involve the loss of life or such restraint of liberty that it's tantamount to loss of life or community. That's our problem today. Our system's shortcomings lead to excessive loss of life and incarceration of such numbers that it devastates communities. This is a recipe for unrest, which will lead to the law being broken.

Some suspect that it's an abortive attempt to use incarceration instead of death to squash subcultures. I think that with a legal system affected by so many people, that's an oversimplification. For some, that has been true since before the Civil War. Others try to combat that attitude. Lately, those others have not been very successful, but that too is an oversimplification. I'll leave that topic for another day, since this is long enough already.

The essence of civilized society is peaceful, voluntary association and trade. Such social co-operation is only possible so far as the principles of private property rights and the non-initiation of force are obeyed. These principles and their applications constitute objective law, determined by the nature of man and of reality.

Only on this conception of law, is it true to say that, "law is the bedrock of civilization." But then talking about "corrupt" or bad laws is nonsense. Objective law may be broken, rejected, misunderstood, or badly enforced. But if it IS valid law, it cannot be wrong.

The "laws" created by state rulers are tools for exploitation and parasitism; they do not promote peaceful social co-operation but hinder it.

It is true that states aim to monopolize crime, and therefore they punish non-state criminals. The phrase "objective law" implies that there is a universal value system to derive that law from. There are places in the world where rape and murder are not considered crimes under certain conditions, legally or colloquially.

This is part of why deities were so useful when civilization was young. Laws could be attributed to an ultimate authority, thus defining objectivity. Ultimately, it was still up to a human being to judge disputes and accusations, so the illusion was strangely thin, considering how well it worked.

When people simply stacked rocks, planted some crops, bartered for sheep, and observed religious practices, it was easy to have a much simpler set of laws. But the more complicated life becomes, the more nuanced the acts that kill or rob become. That calls for more sophisticated laws.
